newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's president warns Bossi not to break law.
newsitem.headline: Italy's president warns Bossi not to break law.

text.p: Italy's President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro warned Northern League leader Umberto Bossi on Sunday that he could face criminal action as the firebrand separatist prepared to proclaim northern "independence".
In a speech at an international trade fair in Bari, southern Italy, Scalfaro said the state intended to guarantee freedom of expression but could not tolerate "incitement to illegal acts".

His warning followed a call by Bossi at a rally on Saturday for volunteers to join a self-styled militia he said he hoped to create after declaring "independence" for his would-be "republic of Padania" in Venice later on Sunday.
"If someone moves to incite illegal acts, the matter then passes into the hands of magistrates," Scalfaro, himself a northerner, said.
"A democracy that was afraid, if the need were to arise, to apply the penal code would not be worthy of continuing to exist," Scalfaro said.

The speech contained some of Scalfaro's most severe criticism of Bossi's secessionist drive, which the Northern League leader is publicising with a symbol-laden journey from the Alpine source of the river Po to the Adriatic Sea.
Though his three-day trek has so far failed to draw the huge crowds he expected, it has had blanket media coverage thanks to Bossi's inflammatory rhetoric.

Magistrates in Turin said on Saturday they had opened inquiries into Bossi's secessionist plans and the role of his green-shirted League "security squad" after formal complaints from individuals and a southern Italian group.

Scalfaro said there was no ethnic basis for secession and noted broad political support for federal reform of the state to answer the frustration with the stifling centralised bureaucracy and inefficiency which Bossi has used to build his following.

"More than 50 million inhabitants, including a strong following in the north of Italy, aren't going to be troubled by a demonstration by thousands of citizens, or perhaps even a million, who do not represent an ethnic minority," Scalfaro said.
